title: Solon Leaves Athens for Ten Years
text:
Around 594 BC Athens was close to civil war. Poor farmers were sinking into debt and many had been enslaved for it, while the wealthy held the land and power. The Athenians gave Solon, a poet and merchant trusted by both sides, special authority to reform the city.

Solon cancelled debts secured on people's freedom, banned enslavement for debt, freed those who had been sold, reorganized the political classes by wealth instead of birth, and wrote a new code of laws. Neither side got everything it wanted. Many urged him to make himself tyrant, and he refused.

Then, according to Herodotus, he did something unusual. The Athenians had sworn to keep his laws for ten years, and Solon left the city for ten years, saying he wanted to see the world. Herodotus says the real reason was to avoid being forced to repeal any of the laws he had made. Plutarch adds that people were pestering him every day with complaints and requests to explain or change his laws, and that he left to let them stand on their own.

He traveled to Egypt, Cyprus and, according to tradition, Lydia, before returning to Athens.
lesson: If you build a system, let it work without you. Stepping away can be the best way to show that rules, not people, are in charge.
source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 1, chapter 29; Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 15 to 26
